meta.description: Not Ingrid Bergman. The definition was in print, unsigned, in 1943 — twenty-seven years before her name was attached to it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Kiss Is A Trick of Nature to Stop Speech When Words Are Superfluous'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Ingrid Bergman since a 1970 newspaper column. It was already in print, anonymous, in Esar's Comic Dictionary of 1943.

answer.label: Not Ingrid Bergman — an anonymous 1943 definition
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known printing is a 1943 entry in Esar’s Comic Dictionary, where it is one of the unsigned comic definitions the compiler Evan Esar described as “of popular origin and therefore unattributed” — so even that book does not claim an author. Ingrid Bergman’s name was attached twenty-seven years later, in a 1970 syndicated column by Hal Boyle that gave no date or occasion for her supposedly saying it. Note too that the 1943 wording is “when words become superfluous”; the “are superfluous” form in circulation today is a later drift.

source.excerpt: kiss. A trick of nature to stop speech when words become superfluous.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ is the anchor here, and its verdict is explicit: “the earliest known instance of this saying appeared in 1943 and was anonymous. The connection to Ingrid Bergman was established at a relatively late date, 1970.”

The 1943 source is given as Esar’s Comic Dictionary, page 154, Harvest House, New York, which QI marks “Verified on paper”. We confirmed the book itself exists — the Internet Archive holds a 1943 scan ↗ — but it is lending-restricted and its text returns an authorisation error, so the page is QI’s reading, not ours.

QI quotes Esar’s own foreword disclaiming authorship of the entries, and complaining about exactly what later happened to this one: “Now more than ever is it a wise crack that knows its own father, for the general practice of apocryphal ascription has been aggravated by the rise of radio.”

Ingrid Bergman’s life dates, 29 August 1915 to 29 August 1982, are confirmed against her Wikipedia entry ↗. She was alive in 1970, so she could in principle have repeated the line — QI allows for that, and for a publicist simply assigning it to her.
source.excerptNote: The 1943 entry as Quote Investigator transcribes it from the book, which it verified on paper. The line was reprinted unsigned for years — the Boston Globe and the Los Angeles Times both ran it as a “Comic Dictionary” item in 1954 — before any name was attached.

source.rightsNote: No rights claim is made here, because there is no identifiable author to hold them. The wording’s origin is unknown, and the earliest printing anyone has produced — the 1943 Comic Dictionary — falls after the 1931 United States public-domain cut-off and carried an Evan Esar copyright notice when the Los Angeles Times reprinted it in 1954. quotle.info therefore makes no public-domain claim for this line.

author.name: Ingrid Bergman
author.heading: About Ingrid Bergman
author.metaLine: 1915–1982 · Swedish actress; three-time Academy Award winner
author.bio: Ingrid Bergman (1915–1982) was a Swedish actress whose career spanned five decades and three Academy Awards, in films from Casablanca and For Whom the Bell Tolls to Autumn Sonata. She is one of the twentieth century’s most quotable screen presences — which is part of the problem here: lines about love and kissing drift toward her name whether or not she ever said them. There is no evidence she originated this one, and the credit appears only in 1970.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Three names get attached to this definition. One is an accident of newspaper filler, one is the man who printed it first and disclaimed it, and one is a columnist who passed it along.

items.why: Her name appears only from 1970, in a syndicated Hal Boyle column ↗ that gave no date, place or occasion — twenty-seven years after the line was already in print unsigned. QI suggests she may have repeated it, or that a publicist simply assigned it to her to make a quotable item.

His 1943 Comic Dictionary is the earliest known appearance, but he printed its definitions unattributed on the stated grounds that they were “of popular origin”, and apologised in advance ↗ for any he had unknowingly borrowed from living writers. Being first in print is not authorship.

Gilbert ran the definition in a 1963 “Daffynitions” column in the Long Island Star-Journal, twenty years after the Comic Dictionary entry, which is sometimes read as a byline for the joke rather than a reprint of it.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: the line was anonymous in 1943 and nobody has produced an author since. The honest credit is unknown.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is a textbook case of how a good line finds a famous mouth. For twenty-seven years the definition circulated as newspaper filler with nobody’s name on it — front pages of the Boston Globe and the Los Angeles Times in 1954, a Schenectady grocery advertisement in 1962. Unsigned filler is unmemorable, and a quotable line wants an owner.

Bergman was a plausible owner: glamorous, articulate, and already associated with a famous comic moment about kissing. Once a 1970 column printed her name under it, later collections copied the column rather than the 1943 book, and the attribution hardened by repetition alone.
context.pull: Unsigned filler is unmemorable, and a quotable line wants an owner.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the earliest known instance of this saying appeared in 1943 and was anonymous, and that the connection to Ingrid Bergman was established only in 1970.
QI cites the 1943 printing as Esar's Comic Dictionary, quote page 154, Harvest House, New York, verified on paper, reading 'kiss. A trick of nature to stop speech when words become superfluous.'
QI quotes Esar's foreword stating the contents were 'of popular origin and therefore unattributed', and his advance apology for any items derived from present-day humorists.
QI documents the 1970 Hal Boyle syndicated column crediting Bergman with 'A kiss is a lovely trick designed by nature to stop speech when words become superfluous.' with no date given for the remark.
The Internet Archive holds a 1943 scan of Esar’s Comic Dictionary; the item is access-restricted and its full text is not readable.
Ingrid Bergman lived 29 August 1915 to 29 August 1982 and was a Swedish actress.
